warmup.q: A table holds a million card payments in 23,818 pages of 8 KB each. (A page is the block a database reads from disk at a time.) Card 4242 has 14 payments, spread across the table. The database also keeps an index on the card number, like the index at the back of a book. About how many pages does it read to find those 14 payments?
options: About 17: a few pages of the index, then one table page per payment
About 1,100: it reads the whole index, which is a twentieth of the table
All 23,818: an index helps put rows in order, not find them
warmup.why: The index is a small tree of pages, three levels deep. The database reads one page at each level, top to bottom, and the bottom page lists the addresses of all 14 payments. Then it reads the table page each payment sits on: 3 + 14 = 17 pages, which the first Try it measures. The first option forgets that the index is made of pages too. The third assumes the whole index is read, which happens only when a query can't be searched in the index's order; the last section shows how easily that happens.

sections.h: One card's payments: every page of the table, or 17 pages through an index
sections.html:
Let's start with a question the payments app answers all day. A small company runs the program that records card payments at shops: which card paid, which shop was paid, how much and when. A customer calls support about a coffee, and the support screen asks for every payment made with card 4242.

The payments live in PostgreSQL, a free database program that many companies run. It keeps them in a table called payments, one row per payment and one column for each detail. The question, written in SQL, the language databases understand, is SELECT ... FROM payments WHERE card_id = 4242: give me these columns of every row whose card is 4242.

On disk, the table is a file cut into pages of 8 KB, the block PostgreSQL reads and writes at a time. The course's large data set has 1,000,478 payments in 23,818 pages, 186 MB in all. PostgreSQL keeps rows in a heap: each new row goes wherever there's room, in no particular order, so card 4242's 14 payments are spread across the file. With nothing else to go on, PostgreSQL can find them only one way. It reads every page and tests every row, which is called a sequential scan.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) in front of a query runs it and prints a report of what PostgreSQL did, called the plan (trimmed, estimates removed):

 Gather (actual time=22.943..249.431 rows=14.00 loops=1)
   Buffers: shared hit=13203 read=10615
   ->  Parallel Seq Scan on payments (actual time=15.929..233.812 rows=4.67 loops=3)
         Filter: (card_id = 4242)
         Rows Removed by Filter: 333488

Each line with a name is a node, one step of the plan. This one read the table from first page to last. Three processes shared the work (loops=3), the main one and two helpers, and Gather collected their rows. rows=4.67 is the average each one found, 14 in all, and each threw away 333,488 rows that didn't match. A buffer is one 8 KB page as EXPLAIN counts it. hit pages were already in PostgreSQL's own memory, and read pages came from the operating system, the program that runs all the others and looks after the disk. That's 23,818 pages for 14 rows, a quarter of a second, and the cost grows with the table.

The cookbook's fix works here too. The book's index lists every ingredient in alphabetical order, with the pages it appears on. Ours lists every card number in order, with the addresses of its rows. A row's address is its page and its slot on that page: card 4242's first payment is at (339,35), row 35 on page 339. PostgreSQL calls this address a ctid.

CREATE INDEX payments_card_idx ON payments (card_id) builds it. PostgreSQL sorts all million card numbers with their addresses and packs them into pages called leaves, 1,130 of them. That's still a lot to search. So above every 283 or so leaves, it adds an inner page that says which card number each leaf starts with, and one root page above those. The result is a B+tree, a tree of pages where each level narrows the search (the lesson B+trees builds one by hand): a root, 4 inner pages and 1,130 leaves.

Card numbers repeat, which keeps the leaves few. Since PostgreSQL 13, a leaf stores a repeated value once, with a sorted list of its addresses, so card 1's entry carries 10. Without that trick (deduplicate_items = off), the same index takes 2,734 leaves and 21 MB instead of 9 MB.

Now card 4242 costs one walk down the tree, root, inner page and leaf, then the 14 table pages its rows are on. That's 17 buffers and a quarter of a millisecond, about a thousand times faster. In Kotlin terms:

val byCard = TreeMap<Long, MutableList<RowAddress>>()   // the index: sorted keys, row addresses
byCard[4242L]                                            // a seek: 3 pages, then 14 addresses
payments.filter { it.cardId == 4242L }                   // no index: test all 1,000,478 rows

That's the picture for the whole lesson. An index is a sorted copy of a few columns, each entry pointing to its row. A query is fast when it can find one short run of entries in that copy. The rest of the lesson asks what lets a query find that run, and what the run costs once it's found. First, we need to read EXPLAIN's report properly.

try.title: A seek instead of a scan
steps: Start PostgreSQL from the labs folder if it isn't running: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait. Docker is a program that runs small separate machines, called containers, on your computer, and this command starts one with PostgreSQL inside. Load the large data set into the course database: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course -f /seed/load-big.sql. It takes about a minute, and earlier lessons of this track ended with down -v, which deleted it. Then open psql, PostgreSQL's program for typing queries: docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course.
Run the block. Read the first plan: how many rows did the scan throw away, and how many buffers did it touch?

The CREATE INDEX takes a few seconds. Compare the second plan's buffers with the first's. The last three queries use pageinspect, an add-on installed in the course database that shows what's inside index pages: check the levels, the pages per level and the sizes.

aside.title: Why not keep the table itself sorted by card number?
aside.html: A table can be in only one order, and the payments app asks by card, by shop and by date. Keeping rows sorted would also mean moving rows to make room whenever a payment lands in the middle. So PostgreSQL leaves the table in arrival order and builds a separate sorted copy for each kind of question that needs one. Some databases do keep the table in the order of one key, and the fourth section shows what that buys and what it costs.

video.title: Index scans, index-only scans and when a sequential scan wins

sections.h: Reading PostgreSQL's report from the bottom up
sections.html:
The first plan had one node. Most plans have several, so let's give the support screen a bigger question. It wants each payment's shop name too, newest payment first. Shop names live in a second table, merchants (the code calls a shop a merchant), so the query joins the two tables: for each payment, it finds the shop row with the same merchant_id. A node that does that, one lookup for each row, is called a Nested Loop.

A plan is a tree. Each node produces rows and hands them to the node above it, and the top node hands them to you. In the text EXPLAIN prints, a node's children sit under it, indented further. So read a plan from the most indented node upward, the way the rows flow. The part of PostgreSQL that picks the plan, before the query runs, is called the planner. The stepper walks through this plan one node at a time. Four kinds of numbers tell you nearly everything:

  • rows is how many rows a node produced each time it ran, and loops is how many times it ran. Multiply them. The merchants Index Scan ran 14 times, once per payment, and found one row each time.
  • Buffers counts the pages a node read, its own and its children's. The Nested Loop's 59 is the payments side's 17 plus the merchants side's 42, so the top node's buffers are the whole query's.
  • cost=4.51..47.94 rows=11 is the planner's estimate, made before the query ran. Cost is in made-up units that only mean something next to other costs. Compare the estimated rows with the actual rows: a miss of ten times or more means the plan was chosen from wrong numbers.
  • Index Cond is a condition PostgreSQL used to search the index. Filter is a condition checked row by row after the rows were read, and Rows Removed by Filter counts the wasted work.

Three kinds of scan node come up all the time. An Index Scan takes each index entry and fetches its row at once, in index order, so its rows come out already sorted. A Bitmap Index Scan first collects every matching row address into a bitmap, a list of yes-or-no marks with one mark per table page. The Bitmap Heap Scan above it then reads each marked page once, in page order. PostgreSQL picks this pair when it expects more than a few rows, or rows on many different pages: here, 14 rows on 14 pages. An Index Only Scan answers from the index alone, without touching the table, and the fourth section shows when that's allowed.

PostgreSQL 18, the version this course uses, changed EXPLAIN in three small ways. EXPLAIN ANALYZE counts buffers without being asked. Rows have two decimals, because they're averages over loops. And each index scan reports Index Searches, how many times it walked down the tree.

One warning before you run anything. Plain EXPLAIN only prints the estimates, so it's safe on any statement. EXPLAIN ANALYZE really runs the statement, and on an UPDATE it changes the rows. So wrap it in BEGIN and ROLLBACK: BEGIN starts a transaction, a group of changes that count together, and ROLLBACK cancels them all.

The shop's own screen asks about two columns at once, and then the order of the columns inside the index decides almost everything. Next, we'll swap them and watch.

sections.h: Two columns in one index: their order decides which questions it answers
sections.html:
Each shop has a screen of its own, a dashboard that shows its 20 newest payments in a month. For shop 1000 in September, the query is:

SELECT payment_id, amount_minor, created_at FROM payments
WHERE merchant_id = 1000 AND created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-10-01'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

ORDER BY created_at DESC puts the newest first, and LIMIT 20 keeps the first 20. Without an index, PostgreSQL reads all 23,818 pages, keeps the 22 payments shop 1000 had in September and sorts them: about 0.7 seconds. An index on both columns fixes it, but the order of the two columns matters a lot.

A good cookbook index shows why. Under "lemon" it has sub-entries, sorted by dish: cake, 112; chicken, 240; tart, 301. Every lemon dish sits together. But the tarts are scattered: one under lemon, one under apple, one under pear. An index on two columns works the same way. It's sorted by its first column, and by the second only among entries with the same first value.

Let's try time first: (created_at, merchant_id). September is now one long run of about 100,000 entries, every shop's payments sorted by time, and shop 1000's entries are scattered through it. PostgreSQL walks the run backward from 1 October and checks each entry's shop until it has 20: 397 pages, 11 ms. That's far better than 0.7 seconds, and it looks fine on a quiet laptop, which is how a wrong order survives.

Now swap them: (merchant_id, created_at). All of shop 1000's entries sit together, already in time order, and its September is one short stretch. PostgreSQL walks down to the last of them and reads 20 entries backward: 23 pages, a tenth of a millisecond. Both plans list both columns under Index Cond, so the condition alone won't tell you which index is good. Judge them by their buffers.

Equality columns first, then the column you range over or sort by. An equality is one exact value, merchant_id = 1000. A range is everything between two values, such as two times. In Kotlin terms, the good index is a TreeMap keyed by compareBy({ it.merchantId }, { it.createdAt }). The range from (1000, 1 September) to (1000, 1 October) is one unbroken subMap. Swap the key's parts, and no unbroken slice holds only shop 1000.

PostgreSQL 18 bends the rule with skip scan. Take an index on (status, created_at), where status is one of three words: succeeded, failed or pending. A query on created_at alone used to get no help from it, because times are sorted only inside each status. Skip scan jumps into each status's part of the index in turn and searches created_at there, like looking for "tart" under each ingredient. For five minutes of payments it reported Index Searches: 7 and read 27 pages, where a sequential scan reads 23,818. It pays only when the first column has few values. Through (merchant_id, created_at), with a shop number first, the same query took 1,616 searches and 5,243 pages.

The Try it has one more plan, and it's the strangest: it reads 4 pages and never touches the table. Next, we'll see how an index can answer a query on its own.

sections.h: Skipping the table: where the rows live, and the index-only scan
sections.html:
Card 4242's lookup ended in the table, with 14 table pages for 14 payments. That's because of where PostgreSQL keeps rows. Its table is a heap, pages in arrival order, and every index on it holds addresses that point into the heap. That includes the index on the primary key, the column that names each row and never repeats (payment_id here). So any lookup is a walk down a tree plus one heap page per row.

MySQL, another popular free database program, makes the other choice in InnoDB, the part of MySQL that stores the data. An InnoDB table is a clustered index: the leaves of the primary key's tree hold the rows themselves. A lookup by primary key ends in the leaf, with nothing more to fetch. Every other index, called a secondary index, stores the row's primary key instead of an address. So a lookup through one walks down two trees, its own and then the primary key's. That's also why a wide primary key, such as a UUID (a random 16-byte id), makes every other index bigger.

Either way, a query can skip the row entirely if the index already holds every column it needs. CREATE INDEX ON payments (merchant_id, created_at) INCLUDE (amount_minor) keeps amount_minor in each leaf entry, carried along but not sorted by. In the cookbook, it's an index that prints the cooking time next to each page number, so some questions never need the page. Now a shop's monthly total can run as an Index Only Scan.

There's a catch, in how PostgreSQL handles changes. It keeps old versions of a changed row for a while, so that a query that started earlier still sees the data as it was. Each version records the transaction that created it and the one that deleted it (fields called t_xmin and t_xmax), and only the heap holds them. An index entry doesn't. So the index alone can't tell whether a row version is one your query should see.

PostgreSQL's answer is the visibility map, two bits for each heap page. One of them says that every row on the page is visible to everyone. Only VACUUM sets it: that's PostgreSQL's clean-up job for row versions nobody can see any more, and autovacuum runs it automatically. Any change to a page clears the bit again. An Index Only Scan skips the heap only for pages with the bit set, and Heap Fetches counts the rows it still had to check in the heap. InnoDB has the same problem: when a secondary index page was changed by a transaction newer than your query, it looks the row up in the clustered index.

The Try it measures both sides. It copies 200,000 payments into a fresh table, first with no index and then with three. The copy with indexes writes 89 MB to the write-ahead log, the file where every change is written first (the previous lesson), against 42 MB without. Before VACUUM no page is all-visible, and the planner doesn't even try an Index Only Scan. After VACUUM, the shop's total reads 4 index pages.

So indexes make reads cheap and writes dearer, and an index the query can't use is all cost. Next, we'll miss an index on purpose and see which small changes cause it.

sections.h: When PostgreSQL can't use an index, and when it chooses not to
sections.html:
An index on created_at is sorted by created_at. It isn't sorted by created_at::date. (The :: is a cast, which turns a value into another type: here, a moment in time into just its day.) Nor is it sorted by lower(email), or by anything else worked out from the column. So PostgreSQL can't search it for those values, just as an index of ingredients can't find recipes by cooking time.

The first miss looks harmless. WHERE created_at::date = '2026-09-01' read the whole index on created_at, 2,739 pages, casting each value and testing it: the plan says Filter, not Index Cond. The same day written as a range on the bare column, created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-09-02', read 13 pages. A condition that can search an index is called sargable, from "search argument". Keep the column alone on one side, and do the arithmetic on the constants.

The second miss comes from the program, not the query. PostgreSQL compares a bigint (a whole number) with a numeric (an exact decimal) by turning the bigint into a numeric. Java programs talk to databases through JDBC, Java's standard database library, and its setBigDecimal call sends a value as numeric. So WHERE payment_id = $1, where $1 is a blank the program fills in, runs as (payment_id)::numeric = $1. The primary key goes unused, and one lookup by id reads all 23,818 pages. Send ids with setLong, which sends a bigint.

When you can't change the query, index the expression itself. A login compares emails without caring about capital letters: WHERE lower(email) = .... CREATE INDEX ON customers (lower(email)) builds an index sorted by exactly that value, and the lookup drops from 532 pages to 4. The expression must be immutable, which means the same input always gives the same result. created_at::date isn't, because the day a moment falls on depends on the connection's time zone setting, so PostgreSQL refuses to index it.

Sometimes the planner skips an index on purpose. 93% of payments are succeeded, so WHERE status = 'succeeded' needs almost every table page anyway. Reading the table straight through beats jumping between index and table 930,000 times, so the plan is a sequential scan even with an index on status. The same index is used for status = 'pending', 1% of rows. If only the rare value is ever asked for, a partial index stores only the rows that match its own condition: CREATE INDEX ON payments (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending' is 232 kB, against 21 MB for an index on created_at over every payment. The planner uses it only when the query's WHERE plainly includes status = 'pending'.

Which indexes are worth their cost on writes? Ask pg_stat_statements, an add-on the course's database loads at start. It records every query shape, with the values replaced by $1, and how often it ran, its total time and the pages it touched. Sort it by total_exec_time, run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) on the top query, and build the index whose first columns are its equality conditions. Then look the other way: pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan counts each index's uses, and one still at 0 after a month only costs writes. And PostgreSQL never indexes a column that points at another table's row, such as payments.merchant_id, for you. Without that index, deleting a shop reads all of payments, to check that no payment still points at it.

Every index in this lesson is one tree of sorted values: numbers, times, names. It answers "equal to", "between" and "starts with", and nothing else. It can't find a word in the middle of a name, the nearest shop on a map or a photo like another one. That's where we go next.

refs.title: Use The Index, Luke: Functions in the WHERE clause

opening:
Picture a cookbook of six hundred pages, and a question: which recipes use lemons? You could turn every page and look. Or you could open the index at the back, find "lemon", and read off six page numbers.

Now ask the same book for every recipe that takes under 20 minutes. The index is no help at all. It's sorted by ingredient, and cooking time isn't in it.

A database works the same way, and it's easy to forget. People add an index, see its column in a slow query, and expect the query to get fast. Often it does. Sometimes the database reads every page anyway, because the index's order can't answer the question, and nothing warns you.

In Write-ahead logging and crash recovery, we made sure a database never loses a change it promised to keep. In this lesson, we'll give a million card payments an index, read the database's report of what it did, and miss the index five ways on purpose. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a cookbook whose index found lemons in six pages and couldn't find a quick dinner at all. A database index is the same deal: a sorted copy that answers the questions its order answers, in 17 pages instead of 23,818, and no help with anything else.

If you have PostgreSQL running, put EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) in front of a query you care about. Look for Index Cond or Filter, and see whether the buffers are in the tens or the thousands.

Next, we'll meet questions a sorted list can't answer: a shop name typed with a mistake, a year of readings by time, the nearest shop on a map, a photo like another one. What does each one need instead?

compare.title: Estimated and actual rows for one query: Oracle and PostgreSQL

a.label: Oracle
a.title: Oracle: run with statistics, then DISPLAY_CURSOR
a.html: -- run the query once, collecting row-source statistics SELECT /*+ gather_plan_statistics */ payment_id, amount_minor, created_at FROM payments WHERE merchant_id = 1000 AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2026-09-01 00:00:00 +00:00' AND created_at < TIMESTAMP '2026-10-01 00:00:00 +00:00' ORDER BY created_at DESC FETCH FIRST 20 ROWS ONLY; -- the plan of this session's last statement, with -- E-Rows (estimated), A-Rows (actual) and Buffers SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR(NULL, NULL, 'ALLSTATS LAST'));

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: PostgreSQL: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)
b.html: -- runs the query and prints the plan with estimated -- and actual rows, loops and buffers on every node -- (BUFFERS is included by default since PostgreSQL 18) EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) SELECT payment_id, amount_minor, created_at FROM payments WHERE merchant_id = 1000 AND created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-10-01' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20; -- plain EXPLAIN: estimates only, nothing runs

compare.note: Oracle Database is a commercial database program that many banks and large firms run. Both databases keep the estimate apart from the measurement. Oracle's EXPLAIN PLAN, like PostgreSQL's plain EXPLAIN, shows only what the planner expects. To see actual rows and pages, Oracle runs the statement with statistics switched on, and DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY_CURSOR then prints its plan, where E-Rows (estimated) against A-Rows (actual) plays the part of PostgreSQL's rows=11 against actual rows=14.00. Both print the plan as an indented tree, read from the innermost line outward. The index rules carry over too. Oracle's B-tree indexes follow the same column-order rule, it has had an index skip scan for many years, and its function-based indexes are PostgreSQL's indexes on expressions. Oracle has no INCLUDE, so a covering index there adds the extra columns to the key.

worked.title: An index for the account statement, from a slow query to an Index Only Scan

steps.say: Every account has a ledger, a table with one row for each change to its balance. The statement page lists one account's ledger entries for a month, oldest first, and pg_stat_statements puts it near the top by total time. On the large data set the ledger has 3,398,299 rows in 33,630 pages, and the plan reads all of them to return 4:
steps.code: -- 1. the query and its plan (EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF), trimmed) SELECT created_at, entry_type, amount_minor FROM ledger_entries WHERE account_id = 4242 AND created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-10-01' ORDER BY created_at; -- Sort (actual time=224.879..229.448 rows=4.00 loops=1) -- Buffers: shared hit=285 read=33348 -- -> Gather -- -> Parallel Seq Scan on ledger_entries (... rows=1.33 loops=3) -- Filter: ((created_at >= ...) AND (created_at < ...) AND (account_id = 4242)) -- Rows Removed by Filter: 1132826

steps.say: Choose the key from the conditions. account_id is an equality, so it goes first. created_at is both the range and the sort order, so it goes second. Then the month is one unbroken run, already in the order the page wants, and the Sort disappears.
steps.code: -- 2. equality column first, then the range and sort column CREATE INDEX ledger_account_created_idx ON ledger_entries (account_id, created_at);

steps.say: The query also returns entry_type and amount_minor. Each one found through the index would still cost a visit to a table page. Carry them in the leaf entries with INCLUDE, so the index alone answers the query.
steps.code: -- 3. the same key, plus the returned columns in the leaves CREATE INDEX ledger_account_created_idx ON ledger_entries (account_id, created_at) INCLUDE (entry_type, amount_minor);

steps.say: Check the plan, not the clock: an Index Only Scan with both conditions under Index Cond, no Sort, no Filter, Heap Fetches: 0 and 7 buffers instead of 33,633. The bill comes with it. On the large data set the index is 161 MB next to a 263 MB table, and it's written on every new ledger entry. For a page every customer opens, that's a fair price. For a report run once a month, it isn't.
steps.code: -- 4. the new plan (EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF), trimmed) -- Index Only Scan using ledger_account_created_idx on ledger_entries (actual time=7.463..7.468 rows=4.00 loops=1) -- Index Cond: ((account_id = 4242) AND (created_at >= ...) AND (created_at < ...)) -- Heap Fetches: 0 -- Index Searches: 1 -- Buffers: shared hit=4 read=3 SELECT pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('ledger_account_created_idx')) AS idx, -- 161 MB pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size('ledger_entries')) AS tbl; -- 263 MB

lab.title: Three indexes and one rewrite, checked against the plan
steps: With Docker running, run the tests from the labs folder. Five of the seven fail. The two that check the rows of payments_on_day already pass, because its placeholder returns the right rows, the slow way.

The tests build a 200,000-row copy of payments once (in schema lab11, already vacuumed), run your statement on it inside a transaction that's rolled back, and read EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS). A failing test prints the whole plan.

WHERE created_at >= timestamptz '2026-03-12 00:00+00' AND created_at < timestamptz '2026-03-13 00:00+00'. The range is half-open, including its start and excluding its end: midnight is in, 23:59:59.5 is in, and the 13th is out.

The query reads merchant_id, created_at, status and amount_minor. Keep the first two as the key and add INCLUDE (status, amount_minor). The second test adds five rows on a page VACUUM hasn't seen, so a few heap fetches are expected there.

drill.title: Pick the index, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the index for each query and say which plan node you expect. (1) WHERE card_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10. (2) WHERE lower(email) = lower(?) on customers. (3) WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at < now() - interval '15 minutes', where 1% of payments are pending. (4) SELECT sum(amount_minor) FROM payments WHERE merchant_id = ? AND created_at >= ? AND created_at < ?. Then rewrite WHERE date_trunc('day', created_at) = '2026-03-12' so an index on created_at can serve it.

answer.html: -- (1) equality, then the sort column: Index Scan Backward, no Sort, stops after 10 CREATE INDEX ON payments (card_id, created_at); -- (2) index the expression the query uses: Index Scan (or Bitmap) with Index Cond on lower(email) CREATE INDEX ON customers (lower(email)); -- (3) a partial index holds only the 1% that is ever queried: small, and an Index Scan CREATE INDEX ON payments (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'; -- (4) key for the search, INCLUDE for the sum: Index Only Scan, Heap Fetches near 0 after VACUUM CREATE INDEX ON payments (merchant_id, created_at) INCLUDE (amount_minor); -- the rewrite: the bare column, a half-open range WHERE created_at >= timestamptz '2026-03-12 00:00+00' AND created_at < timestamptz '2026-03-13 00:00+00'

recap: An index is a sorted copy of a few columns, each entry holding its row's address, kept as a B+tree of pages. Three levels find card 4242's entries in 3 page reads, then one table page per row: 17 pages, where a sequential scan reads all 23,818.

Read EXPLAIN from the most indented node up. Multiply rows by loops, remember that a node's buffers include its children's, and compare estimated rows with actual rows. An Index Cond searches the index; a Filter only throws rows away.
In an index on several columns, put the equality columns first, then the column you range over or sort by. PostgreSQL 18's skip scan helps only when the first column has few values.

PostgreSQL's indexes point into the heap. InnoDB's table is its primary key's tree, and its other indexes hold the primary key. INCLUDE columns allow an Index Only Scan, which skips only the pages VACUUM marked all-visible: watch Heap Fetches.

A cast or function on the column, or a value of another type sent by the program, stops the index search: keep the bare column on one side, or index the expression. A condition most rows match is rightly read with a scan, and a partial index covers the rare values.

The limit: every index is written on every insert and most updates (three indexes doubled the log), and a B+tree only answers questions about its one sort order. Choose indexes from pg_stat_statements, and drop the ones nobody uses.

explain.prompt: A teammate added an index on payments(created_at) for the daily report, which filters with WHERE created_at::date = :day, and the report is as slow as before. Explain what's happening, what you would change, and how you would prove the fix with EXPLAIN.
explain.answer: The index is a sorted copy of the created_at values. The report compares created_at::date, a day worked out from each row, and the index isn't sorted by that, so PostgreSQL can't jump to the day's first entry. It either scans the table or reads the whole index and casts every value. The plan shows the condition as a Filter with hundreds of thousands of rows removed: on the course's large data set, that was 2,739 pages for one day. An index on the expression would fix the search, but created_at::date depends on the session's time zone, so PostgreSQL refuses to build it. The clean fix is to rewrite the condition as a half-open range on the bare column, created_at >= :day and created_at < :day + 1, with the two edges worked out in the program, in UTC or in the business's own time zone. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) then shows an Index Scan or Index Only Scan with both edges under Index Cond, no Filter on created_at, and buffers in the tens: 13 pages in the course's run. I'd check it on a table of real size, because on a small table every plan looks fast.

deeper.html:
BRIN is a different kind of index, for tables whose rows sit on disk in the order of one column. It stores only the smallest and largest value for each range of pages, 128 pages by default. Payments were inserted in time order, so a BRIN index on payments(created_at) is 24 kB instead of 21 MB, and a query for a time range skips every page range that can't match. It's useless when the order is mixed, as it is for ledger_entries.created_at in the large data set, which was loaded one entry type at a time. pg_stats.correlation tells you which case you're in: 0.999 for payments.created_at, 0.314 for the ledger's. Near 1 or -1 suits BRIN.

GIN, from the SQL track's lesson JSONB, upserts and MERGE, is an inverted index: one entry for each key or value found inside a document or list, each with the rows that contain it. It answers containment questions such as @>, and it pays for that on writes. Its fastupdate list of pending entries hides part of that cost until VACUUM, or a full list, merges them in.

The planner's estimates come from statistics that ANALYZE (and autovacuum) collect: a sample of each column's values, its most common values, a histogram and the number of distinct values. When two columns go together, say a shop and its country, the planner multiplies their chances as if they were unrelated, and guesses too few rows. CREATE STATISTICS on the pair fixes that. Lesson 10 of this track, Query optimization and cardinality estimates, builds the estimator itself.

Writes differ between the two designs too. A PostgreSQL update writes a new version of the row. If an indexed column changed, or the new version can't stay on the same page, every index gets a new entry, even indexes on columns nobody touched. When neither happens, PostgreSQL skips the index work, a shortcut called a HOT update. An InnoDB update that changes no indexed column touches only the clustered index, because the other indexes point at a primary key that didn't move.

A partial index has one more trap. The planner must prove, while it plans, that the query's WHERE implies the index's. status = 'pending' written into the query does. status = $1 in a prepared statement (a query sent once with blanks, then run many times) doesn't, once PostgreSQL switches to a generic plan, one plan for every value, because the value isn't known yet.

Oracle Database has its own version of the type trap. A column of one text type (VARCHAR2) compared with a value of another (NVARCHAR) sent by the program gets converted, and its index goes unused.

On a busy table, CREATE INDEX blocks writes for as long as it runs. CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY doesn't, at the price of two passes over the table and the rule that it can't run inside a transaction. So a migration that uses it (a numbered script that changes the database, from SQL from the JVM) must be marked to run outside one. If it fails halfway, it leaves an INVALID index behind that you have to drop.

auto_explain writes the plan of every statement slower than a threshold to the database's log, with auto_explain.log_analyze for actual rows. It's how you catch the plan of a query that's only slow on the real system, at 3 a.m., with that day's data.
